headline: The TS journey is a diagnosis-to-specialist-to-treatment funnel — caregiver-mediated, school-involved, and slowed by underdiagnosis — not an infusion journey.

stages.title: Symptom onset
stages.detail: First symptoms usually motor tics (~56%), often mistaken for allergies, vision problems, or behavior. Onset preschool (~40%) or early primary school (~36%).

stages.title: First contact
stages.detail: Clear-cut cases may be recognized here; many are not. Comorbid ADHD/OCD/anxiety frequently surface first and steer the workup.

stages.title: Referral churn & diagnostic delay
stages.detail: Parents consult ~4 different types of professional before diagnosis; delay often runs years. TS is a clinical diagnosis (no confirmatory test) — once the right specialist is reached, diagnosis is usually quick.

stages.title: Specialist diagnosis
stages.who: Pediatric neurology / movement-disorder specialist (secondarily child psychiatry)
stages.detail: Confirmation, severity staging (YGTSS), and the point where tic-specific pharmacotherapy is initiated. This is the commercial call-point that matters most.

stages.title: Treatment decision
stages.detail: Watchful waiting for non-impairing tics; CBIT and/or pharmacotherapy for impairing tics. Caregivers, IEP/504 school supports, and comorbidity management all shape the choice.

leak_points.label: Underdiagnosis
leak_points.detail: ~half of children with TS are never formally diagnosed.

leak_points.label: Diagnostic delay
leak_points.detail: ~4 clinicians and often years before diagnosis.

leak_points.label: Comorbidity capture
leak_points.detail: ADHD/OCD/anxiety often treated first; the tic conversation happens in a crowded context.

leak_points.label: CBIT access
leak_points.detail: First-line CBIT is frequently unavailable in practice (therapist shortage).

ecosystem.title: A caregiver- and school-mediated condition
ecosystem.note: Unlike an adult specialty launch, the TS decision unit includes parents/caregivers, schools (IEP/504 accommodations under IDEA/ADA), and often counselors — all motivated for the child to do well. Advocacy is TAA-centric.
